title: Stable valleys in the glassy landscape of a low-density parity-check (LDPC) code
authors: Grace M. Sommers, David A. Huse
abstract: Classical low-density parity-check (cLDPC) codes defined on expander graphs are a fundamental ingredient in the construction of good quantum LDPC codes, a recent milestone in quantum error correction. They also define interesting statistical mechanics models in their own right, as they include examples of spin glass order without quenched randomness or frustration. We investigate this via a case study of a cLDPC code on a locally tree-like expander graph. Recursive techniques on trees, made possible by the locally tree-like property, probe a menagerie of stable, incongruent valleys induced by imposing different boundary conditions at low temperature. A complementary numerical study of the valleys on closed finite graphs reveals the inequivalence of the microcanonical and canonical ensemble for certain valleys.
summary: This paper analyzes the rugged energy landscape of LDPC codes, treating them as a model for spin glass physics. It uses advanced statistical mechanics sampling techniques to characterize metastable 'valleys' within this landscape. The key finding is the demonstration of ensemble inequivalence, showing that standard thermodynamic relations break down when analyzing these glassy states.
main_problem: The study investigates stable valleys within the complex, glassy energy landscape of a low-density parity-check (LDPC) code.
main_result: The work demonstrates that ensemble inequivalence can occur in these systems, specifically identifying regimes where valleys are microcanonically stable but canonically unstable.
method: The analysis employs advanced sampling techniques like the multicanonical method and adaptive Monte Carlo simulations to probe energy barriers and entropy landscapes.
model_or_system: The system is a classical LDPC code defined on expander graphs, which models spin glass order without explicit quenched randomness. The Hamiltonian penalizes local configurations that violate the code constraints.
key_observables: Bulk free energy density ($f$), energy density ($\epsilon$), configurational entropy density ($s_{	ext{conf}}$), and the height of the entropy barrier ($\Delta S$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($ eta$ or $T$), boundary condition parameters $(\alpha, \gamma)$, and minimum/maximum allowed values for energy ($E$) or magnetization ($M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximating the true entropy barrier by projecting the configuration space onto a single coordinate (like magnetization $M$), which is noted as a potential source of error.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate comparisons between energy densities derived from different boundary conditions and show phase diagrams mapping out regions of canonical instability versus microcanonical stability.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using tree recursion, then applying advanced sampling methods (multicanonical) to characterize valleys, and finally comparing results across ensembles to pinpoint ensemble inequivalence boundaries.
why_interesting: While focused on coding theory, the mathematical machinery developed—analyzing glassy dynamics, phase transitions, and ensemble equivalence in complex energy landscapes—is directly applicable to understanding many-body systems like spin glasses or frustrated quantum magnets.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The LDPC code studied in this work is defined on a high-girth random regular graph, where the external thin gray lines schematically indicate randomly closed boundaries. Each vertex (orange square) is satisfied if the neighboring bits (blue circles) belong to the code space of the chosen local code, with parity check matrix HL. Here we take the local code to be the Hamming [7,4,3] code. Adapted from Fig. 5 of Ref. [35].)

FIG. 2. Bulk energy density for valleys induced by various fine-tuned boundary conditions (orange and green curves). Also shown is the paramagnetic energy density εpara (black curve) and the energy density within codeword valleys (γ = ∞, blue curve). Star marks (TG, εG). Shading is conjectured region of thermally stable valleys that can be accessed with fine-tuned boundary conditions.

FIG. 3. (a) Heuristic phases of stability for valleys parameterized by εmin, where εmin is the energy density at the bottom of the valley. Horizontal blue line marks the energy density at which a valley has a “canonical instability”, manifesting as a local maximum in x(E) in panel (b). Shaded gray region marks the regime where the valley is canonically unstable, but microcanonically stable due to an extensive entropy barrier to escape from the valley at that energy. Thick light blue curve is a rough estimate of the energy at which the entropic barrier vanishes.
